claims.text: Premelting onset and progression in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are dominated by nanoscale compositional heterogeneity rather than by particle-size effects alone.
Heat-treatment-induced surface segregation is the specific compositional heterogeneity governing premelting behavior.
The baseline nanoparticles are compositionally uniform, as-synthesized HEA nanoparticles with sizes of 5–20 nm.
HEA nanoparticles can exhibit compositional heterogeneity associated with synthesis.
Controlled post-synthesis heat treatments can enhance or suppress surface chemical segregation while particle size remains constant.
Surface compositional heterogeneity and local atomic ordering can vary in multicomponent alloys.
Elevated temperatures increase atomic mobility in the nanoparticles.
Heat-treatment-induced atomic mobility causes preferential segregation of particular elements at nanoparticle surfaces.
Surface compositional inhomogeneity creates locally weakly bonded regions.
Weakly bonded surface regions lower the energy barrier for local premelting.
Regions with greater segregation have lower premelting and eventual melting temperatures than uniformly mixed regions or particles.
Nanoparticles with greater induced surface segregation will show a measurable reduction in premelting onset temperature relative to homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with greater induced surface segregation will melt more gradually than homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
The predicted segregation-controlled behavior should hold for HEA nanoparticles between 5 and 20 nm when size effects are held constant.
The predicted behavior should extend across multicomponent alloys with similar configurational complexity.
Substrate interactions, ligands, and environmental conditions may alter segregation and premelting behavior.
DSC can identify the onset temperature of premelting in the proposed nanoparticles.
TEM/EDS can directly quantify the relevant surface segregation patterns in the proposed nanoparticles.
